claims.text: Jobs and Steve Wozniak started Apple in Jobs's parents' garage when Jobs was 20
In about ten years Apple grew into a $2 billion company with more than 4,000 employees
In April 1985 Sculley told the board he would resign unless Jobs was removed as head of the Macintosh division; the board backed Sculley
At the end of May 1985 Jobs was stripped of every operating role; he kept only the title of chairman
In the same weeks Apple cut 20% of its workforce, announced its first-ever quarterly loss, and its stock hit a three-year low
Sculley told analysts: "There is no role for Steve Jobs in the running of this company, either today or in the future"
In September 1985 Jobs resigned as chairman, saying the board had made his plans "a very hostile situation"
He was 30 years old

Jobs said he was out "very publicly", thought about leaving Silicon Valley, and later called the firing "the best thing that could have ever happened to me" and spoke of "the lightness of being a beginner again"
He founded NeXT after leaving Apple in 1985

In February 1986 Jobs paid Lucasfilm $5 million for the graphics group's technology and put another $5 million into the new company, Pixar; Ed Catmull ran it day to day; its first product was a high-end image computer for medical imaging and film effects
Over the following years Jobs put about $50 million of his own money into Pixar
NeXT lost between $40 million and $66 million a year for three straight years before a $1.03 million profit in 1994
NeXT's computers struggled to find a market and NeXT stopped making its own hardware
Toy Story, the first computer-animated feature film, opened on 22 Nov 1995 and became the year's top-grossing film
Pixar went public on 29 Nov 1995 at $22 a share and closed its first day at $39; Jobs owned about 80%, which made him a billionaire
On 20 Dec 1996 Apple announced it would buy NeXT, a deal first announced at $400 million; it closed on 7 Feb 1997 at roughly $427–429 million in cash and stock
Jobs came back as an adviser to CEO Gil Amelio
On 6 Aug 1997 at Macworld Boston, Jobs announced Microsoft would invest $150 million in non-voting Apple stock and keep making Office for the Mac
Jobs became interim CEO in September 1997
On 6 Oct 1997 Michael Dell, asked what he would do with Apple, said: "I'd shut it down and give the money back to the shareholders"
Apple lost $1.05 billion in fiscal 1997 on about $7 billion of revenue

claims.text: Technology built at NeXT became the heart of Apple's later revival
Pixar's first feature was made under a deal with Disney, which released it
Gil Amelio left as Apple's CEO in July 1997 after a $56 million quarterly loss; Apple lost about $1.6B under him and announced about 3,000 job cuts
Apple's own next-generation operating system (Copland) had been abandoned and it needed a replacement
Some of the Macworld audience booed the Microsoft announcement
In 2018 Apple became the first US company valued at $1 trillion
Steve Wozniak resigned from Apple in February 1985
Jobs recruited Sculley from the presidency of Pepsi-Cola USA in 1983
At the start of 1985 Jobs owned about 11.3% of Apple, worth around $120 million
NYT, Feb 1986: Pixar had 43 employees; Jobs chairman, Catmull runs daily operations; Jobs said image computing "will explode"
Luxo Jr. (1986) was nominated for an Oscar; Tin Toy won one
In 1991 Jobs shut down Pixar's applications-software effort
Pixar CFO Lawrence Levy, who arrived in late 1994, has said he quickly realised the company was doomed
During those years he met his future wife
NeXT drafted (never filed) an IPO S-1 in Nov 1996; by 1996 NeXT's newest software products (WebObjects, OPENSTEP for Windows) brought in $10.1M, about 45% of sales
Toy Story took $29M in its opening weekend and grossed about $362M worldwide
After the IPO, Jobs negotiated a new five-picture Disney deal giving Pixar an equal share of profits
Apple cut inventory from about $400M to $78M — about six days' supply — by the end of fiscal 1998
Apple's "Think Different" campaign featured figures such as Einstein, Miles Davis and John Lennon; 1998 ad budget over $100M
Apple said about 30% of iMac buyers were new to Apple and 12% had switched from Windows
Disney bought Pixar in 2006 in an all-stock deal worth $7.4B, leaving Jobs with about 7% of Disney
NeXT's first computer, the cube, was introduced in 1988
Pixar's IPO roadshow screened Toy Story for investors and their families in a rented New York theatre, and a blizzard forced an all-night drive to Boston
Gil Amelio said "I'm not just buying software, I'm buying Steve"

claims.text: Joanne Rowling was born on 31 July 1965 in Yate, England
In 1990 the idea for Harry Potter came to her on a delayed train; she was stuck for about four hours with nothing to write on
She was an Exeter University graduate working in London, including for Amnesty International, when she started the books
Her mother, Anne, had multiple sclerosis and died in 1990, aged 45
She had begun writing the first book months before her mother died (The Guardian says six; the Telegraph, three)
She moved to northern Portugal to teach English (afternoons and evenings, writing in the mornings), married Jorge Arantes in 1992 and had a daughter, Jessica, in 1993
The marriage broke up when Jessica was about three and a half months old; Rowling went to stay with her younger sister, Di, in Edinburgh at Christmas 1993
She arrived with the first three chapters of Harry Potter
In Edinburgh she lived on state benefits (income support)
Harvard, 5 Jun 2008: seven years after graduating, her short marriage "had imploded"; she was jobless, a lone parent, and "as poor as it is possible to be in modern Britain, without being homeless"
Harvard: by every usual measure she was "the biggest failure I knew"; failure was "a stripping away of the inessential"; rock bottom became "the solid foundation on which I rebuilt my life"
She has said: "Depression is the most unpleasant thing I have ever experienced"
She wrote much of the first book in Edinburgh cafés
The Christopher Little Literary Agency took her on after a reader there liked the first three chapters
Little took about a year to find a publisher; the manuscript was turned down by twelve publishers (the widely reported figure; she has never named them)
Bloomsbury chairman Nigel Newton took the sample home and gave it to his eight-year-old daughter, Alice, who came back about an hour later asking for more
Editor Barry Cunningham championed the book and Bloomsbury's children's list took it on
Bloomsbury asked for initials so boys would not be put off by a woman's name; she had no middle name and added K for her grandmother Kathleen
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone was published on 26 June 1997
The first hardback print run was 500 copies, about 300 of them for libraries
The Scottish Arts Council gave her £8,000, its largest award to a children's writer, which she spent partly on a word processor; the second book, Chamber of Secrets, was published in 1998
Scholastic won a US auction for the rights at $105,000; she said "I nearly died" when told
Hollywood studios competed for the film rights within weeks; Warner Bros. later bought rights to the first two books
The series (seven books, eight films, a stage play) has sold more than 500 million copies (figure reached by 2022)
She became an ambassador for One Parent Families (now Gingerbread) and its president in 2007
The Anne Rowling Regenerative Neurology Clinic in Edinburgh, named after her mother, opened in 2013
She gave the Harvard commencement address on 5 June 2008

Her parents, from poor backgrounds, wanted a practical degree; her imagination "would never pay a mortgage, or secure a pension"; she studied Modern Languages, then Classics; what she feared most "was not poverty, but failure"
In her early twenties she worked in Amnesty International's African research department in London, read smuggled letters and torture testimony, and said it gave her "literal nightmares"
By 1990 she worked in an office job in Manchester; the train was from Manchester to London
She said she felt guilty about not being there when her mother died, and her mother never read her writing
In Edinburgh she told her sister Di the story; Di's laughter encouraged her to keep going
She said there were nights she skipped meals so Jessica could eat; life on benefits was "soul-destroying"; she had "no intention, no desire, to remain on benefits"; she worried about a "poverty trap"
She wrote longhand at Nicolson's café in Edinburgh while Jessica slept, ordering espresso and water; writing "really saved my sanity"; she later took a part-time job

Harvard: a life is not a checklist of acquisition or achievement; failure showed her a strong will and more discipline than she suspected, friends "truly above the price of rubies"; imagination's most important use is empathy; "We do not need magic to change the world"
She named her daughter after Jessica Mitford, whose sense of humour she admired
A former library copy of the first-edition hardback later sold at auction for $88,140
The £8,000 grant was more than triple her advance; the US auction involved about ten publishers

claims.text: Tyler Perry was born in 1969 and grew up in New Orleans
His mother grew up in the Jim Crow South; he has described growing up with an abusive, alcoholic father in an area marked by poverty, and credits his mother, aunts and grandmother
He dropped out of high school
After watching Oprah Winfrey talk about writing as a way to work through pain, he began writing letters to himself, which became the basis of his first play, I Know I've Been Changed
The play was about survivors of child abuse and the power of prayer
He moved to Atlanta to launch the play
He worked as a bill collector, sold used cars and worked in hotels, and saved $12,000, including a tax refund
In 1992 he spent all of it renting a theatre space and staging the play in Atlanta; he expected 1,200 people that weekend and about 30 came
His rent and car payment were tied up in it and he ended up homeless
"For three months, I lived in a Geo Metro that I was hiding from the repo man"; he is six foot five
Over those years he was homeless on and off, including living in a pay-by-the-week hotel
He took jobs between attempts and quit each time to work on the play
He staged the play about once a year — 1992, 1993, 1994 — and "every year it would fail, until 1998, the seventh year"; he was about to give up
Audience members told him the play had changed their lives, and he began to see the value of serving others
In 1998 he staged it again at the House of Blues in Atlanta; it became a hit and he toured it from 1998 to 2000, filling theatres
He has said the show saved his life and "gave me permission to heal"
He created Madea (played by Perry himself in drag) in the 2000 play I Can Do Bad All by Myself
Diary of a Mad Black Woman (2005), the first film made from his plays, opened at No. 1 in the US and introduced Madea to mainstream audiences
Madea's Family Reunion opened at No. 1 with $30.3 million in February 2006
In 2015 he bought 330 acres of the former Fort McPherson army post (488 acres in all) for $30 million
Part of that land was once used as a Confederate army base
He has said he buried Bibles beneath the soundstages

He estimated his total investment at about $250 million; the lot has 12 soundstages and about 200 acres of green space, including historic homes on the old officers' row and a full-scale White House set
For comparison, Warner Bros.' Burbank studio lot is about 110 acres
The studio's grand opening gala was on 5 Oct 2019
It is widely reported as making him the first African American to own a major film studio outright
The studio hosted a 2020 Democratic presidential debate in November 2019
The studio provides hundreds of production jobs, including for former prisoners
Forbes estimated him a billionaire in 2020
He still takes a Geo Metro out now and then as a reminder of the car he once lived in, and posted that looking back at how far you've come should make you thankful
"If you find the lessons in what you perceive to be failures, then you won't ever fail at anything"
He says "I just did the work", that he had "no other choice than to follow my dream", and that his humility comes from remembering that car
Oprah Winfrey later became his business partner and his son's godmother
His first two Madea films earned back their production budgets about ten times over
As a small child he imitated the women his mother played cards with, to make her laugh
His entrepreneurial style clashed with the studio system; in 2006 he self-financed 10 episodes of House of Payne and tested them on a handful of stations

TBS ordered an unprecedented 100 episodes; Perry owned the rights ("Tyler Perry owns all the rights and we distribute it" — Debmar-Mercury); he delivered 100 episodes in one calendar year at his Atlanta studio; the first run totalled 254 episodes

BET Awards, 23 Jun 2019: he said Confederate soldiers had once planned on that ground how to keep millions enslaved, and "Now that land is owned by one Negro"; closed with "Own your stuff, own your business, own your way" and "rather than being an icon, I want to be an inspiration"; presenter Taraji P. Henson said he was "the first to pay me my exact worth"
Between attempts he worked odd jobs while revising the show
He has advised creators to build their base inside their own community first, saying Lionsgate would not have dealt with him had he not grown it "homegrown first"
Black Panther was the first film shot on the new stages
Some residents near the old base were frustrated and questioned how much the studio gives back; the redevelopment authority said it was listening

Network sitcoms typically take nearly five seasons to reach 100 episodes, when syndication deals become possible; in 2007 he said "coming off being homeless, I wanted something that would speak to people"
Forbes's 2020 breakdown of his fortune included cash and investments, his BET+ stake and Tyler Perry Studios
